Subject: Clarify pricing structures: per-token vs reserved capacity vs private deploy — next steps

Hi Ella / Tom,

Thanks again for the call earlier — useful to understand Skylab's immediate use case (document summarization + reranking for analytics queries) and the constraint window around PII / data residency. I promised a short follow-up to align on what we need to run clean cost comparisons across three options: Hosted API, Dedicated (reserved capacity), and Private (VPC/on-prem).

Quick recap of what I heard:
- Workload: ~30M tokens/day average, ~200 QPS peak; median request ~700 tokens, tail up to 2k tokens when doing long-context summaries.
- Latency SLO: 300–500ms P95 for inferencing responses is ideal; some async batch is OK for nightly jobs.
- Data: customer PII stays in their VPC; they want to avoid sending raw logs off-prem for audit reasons unless encrypted and retained <90 days.
- Timing: procurement kicks off in 6–8 weeks; pilot desired in next 4–6 weeks.

To produce useful TCO scenarios I need the following items from you (short bullets are fine):
1) Expected sustained tokens/day and expected peak tokens/sec (or QPS) during business hours.
2) Percent of requests requiring >1024 tokens (estimate).
3) Any mandatory compliance items that force on-prem or KMS-managed keys.
4) Internal decision owners and procurement lead + timeline for a 6–12 month commit.

Next steps I propose:
- You send the bullets above.
- We run three scenario models (per-token hosted, reserved GPU commit for Dedicated, and Private deployment CAPEX/OPEX run-rate). We’ll surface: unit economics (per effective 1k tokens), required commit, expected burn for a 6-month pilot, and infra assumptions (batching, KV cache hits, quantization uplift).
- I’ll loop Marissa (pricing) and Karthik (solutions) to prepare a short spreadsheet and a draft pilot SOW.

Is all that aligned? If yes, send the numbers and I’ll get a first-pass back in 48 business hours.

Thanks,
Jonas

Jonas / Karthik — attached is the first-pass TCO (spreadsheet) and a short summary. High-level takeaways:

Summary (short):
- For Skylab's mix (30M tokens/day, 18% long requests, target P95 300–500ms): a 6-month Dedicated reserved commit (mid-size GPU pool with 30% burst buffer) yields ~35–45% cost savings vs pure Hosted at current per-token list, assuming 40% KV cache hit and batching optimizations.
- Hosted remains simplest for pilot (fastest time-to-value) — expected monthly burn for a 6-month pilot: ~$58k–$72k/mo depending on profile.
- Dedicated commit: recommended commit band = 150k GPU-hours/month (mapped to our mid-tier nodes) — effective per-1k-token cost drops below hosted at ~25M tokens/day sustained. 3-month commit less attractive; 12-month offers incremental discount but locks them in.
- Private (on-prem): large upfront CAPEX (~$450k–$700k depending on redundancy/KMS appliances) and ~20–30% higher ops run-rate vs Dedicated; justified if Skylab insists on full data locality and audit controls.

Key assumptions included in the sheet: per-GPU throughput for our mid-tier SKU, average tokens generated per request (700), avg KV cache hit 40%, batching saves ~18% token cost on average, egress/KMS estimated at $0.015/token-equivalent for persisted logs. I called out sensitivity ranges in the attached tabs.

Recommendation / next steps:
1) Run a short pilot on Hosted with an operational SLO and a backfill plan to Dedicated if sustained load crosses the indicated thresholds. This minimizes procurement friction and shortens time-to-data.
2) Prepare a 6-month Dedicated commit proposal sized to Skylab's projected sustained tokens with an opt-out clause if they fail to meet the commit by >30% for two consecutive months.
3) If Skylab's security team requires customer-managed KMS + full log locality, we should scope a Private deployment and present a detailed certification plan (separate cost and timeline).

Deliverables attached: estimated-tco-vs-commit.xlsx, draft-map-pilot-sow.pdf. I also linked a short talk track.

I’ll be available Tuesday if you want to rehearse the numbers before the customer call.

Marissa Cole
